Every phase of movement, every small transfer of weight, every single gesture … reveals some feature of our inner life.

Master Lecture · Dance, cinema and fashion

A dance that never stops — stopped

Describe · Forms

Bodies, gown, light, crop. Where does the line of the dress go, and where does it stop?

Production

A publicity still, not a film frame. Who posed it, for whom?

Critical

Who leans and who holds? What does the photo freeze that the dance never would?

Image: Ginger Rogers in a feathered gown leans back in Fred Astaire’s arm; he wears white tie and tails.

  • Model step 1–3 aloud, then let pairs do 6–8.
  • Point at the feathered sleeve: the costume is built to be seen in motion.

Master Lecture · Dance, cinema and fashion

1 · The cloth arrives after the body

A garment is not a costume until it moves — and we feel that movement in our own body.

we map these postures and gestures onto our own body, feeling them in our own skin and bones

(Shinkle 2008, 222)

Watch the Muybridge loop in the lesson: the hem lands after the step.

Image: Isadora Duncan, barefoot, in a loose tunic, one arm raised against a dark ground.

Isadora Duncan dancing LOC agc.7a09881 · Arnold Genthe · Public domain · Source

  • Very little film of Duncan dancing is known: her dance reaches us through stills.
  • Ask: which 'classical' body becomes the ideal here, and who is left out?

Master Lecture · Dance, cinema and fashion

2 · A borrowed antiquity

Fortuny's pleated Delphos — made by a designer born in Granada — and Duncan's tunic both borrow an idea of ancient Greece.

Museo del Traje, Madrid · MT111885. You can visit it.

Image: A long black finely pleated silk Delphos gown on a mannequin.

Museo del Traje - MT111885 - Vestido Delphos · Museo del Traje (photograph); Mariano Fortuny y Madrazo (gown) · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Source

  • Drape: the garment follows and lengthens the gesture.
  • Revival is not the ancient practice itself: what evidence would tell them apart?

Master Lecture · Dance, cinema and fashion

3 · A patent for flying cloth

Loïe Fuller patented a 'garment for dancers' in 1894: a skirt hung from the head, thrown into waves with wands.

Open the 1894 patent (US 518,347)

Image: Loose painted sketch: a figure almost disappears inside green, white and violet swirls of cloth.

(Albi) - La Loïe Fuller aux-Folies-Bergère - Toulouse-Lautrec (1893) MTL.152 · Henri de Toulouse-Lautrec · Public domain · Source

  • Extension: the costume becomes the image.
  • Ask: who gets the authorship credit — dancer, maker, or patent holder?

Master Lecture · Dance, cinema and fashion

4 · Most 'Fuller' films show someone else

The serpentine dance was copied everywhere: Annabelle for Edison, an unnamed dancer for Lumière, a Pathé copy coloured in Barcelona.

Play the three films in the lesson

Image: A dancer outdoors swings a long sheer scarf in a wide arc above her head.

Loie Fuller dancing with scarf · Unknown photographer · Public domain · Source

  • Watch the films as evidence, not illustration.
  • The Pathé card says 1902, Commons says 1901: dates disagree. Keep that tension.

Master Lecture · Dance, cinema and fashion

5 · The dancer draws lines

Kandinsky's Bauhaus notebook gives you a looking tool for every clip today.

The entire body of the dancer, right down to his finger tips, is at every moment an uninterrupted composition of lines

(Kandinsky 2012, “Line”)

Image: Three of Isadora Duncan’s dancers in tunics hold a veil above a seated figure.

Isadora Duncan dancers LOC agc.7a10003 · Arnold Genthe · Public domain · Source

  • Kandinsky credits the observation to the dancer Gret Palucca.
  • Trace one line in the image with your finger before speaking.

Master Lecture · Dance, cinema and fashion

6 · Start from the step

Schlemmer did not start from geometry but from a body standing on a stage.

Puesto que dar un paso es un acontecimiento grandioso, mientras que levantar una mano, mover un dedo, no lo son menos.

(Schlemmer 1987, 112)

“For taking a step is a grand event — and raising a hand or moving a finger no less.”

Image: Printed programme of the Triadic Ballet premiere listing twelve dances in yellow, pink and black series.

Das Triadische Ballett, Programmzettel 1922 · Oskar Schlemmer · Public domain · Source

  • Premiere: Stuttgart, 30 September 1922.
  • This is a document, not a photograph of the premiere.

Master Lecture · Dance, cinema and fashion

7 · Geometry decides the step

Rigid, geometric figures reorganise the body: some steps become impossible, new ones appear.

Image: Triadic Ballet figures on a tiled stage: a spiked conical skirt, a club-like arm, a ballooning dark form.

Oskar Schlemmer Triadisches Ballett 200 · Oskar Schlemmer (figures); photographer not identified · Public domain · Source

  • Reorganisation: the costume dictates the choreography.
  • Bridge to Lab C4: build a constraint and film what it forces.

Master Lecture · Dance, cinema and fashion

8 · What does the garment do to movement?

Drape, extension, tension, reorganisation: a map to argue with, not a fact.

Image: Museum display of three Triadic Ballet figures on low plinths against dark walls.

Triadisches Ballett by Oskar Schlemmer - Staatsgalerie - Stuttgart - Germany 2017 · José Luiz Bernardes Ribeiro (photograph); Oskar Schlemmer (figures) · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Source

  • Place each clip and image on the map; defend with one frame.
  • Museum display ≠ performance.

What does the garment do to movement?

  • Place each clip and image on the map; defend with one frame.
  • It is a course hypothesis, not a fact.

Master Lecture · Dance, cinema and fashion

9 · The body pushes against the cloth

In Graham's Lamentation a stretched jersey tube turns grief into visible tension.

Watch Night Journey in the lesson

Image: A seated dancer wrapped in a stretched tube of pale fabric; only face, hands and feet show.

Janet Eilber Performing Martha Graham’s “Lamentation” in the East Room of the White House - NARA - 30805967 · White House photographer (US National Archives) · Rights under review · Source

  • Tension: the garment resists, the body works against it.
  • Then Night Journey: when does the long skirt move with the body, when against it?

Master Lecture · Dance, cinema and fashion

10 · Same dance, different film

A camera chooses a frame, a distance and a cut — and still clings to the moving body.

Cameras will, with all their complex technical possibilities, in most cases still cling to and follow concrete body movements.

(Pfeiffer 2009, 198)

Image: Rogers in a full ruffled gown and Astaire in tails dance; her skirt flares wide.

Swing Time (1936) · RKO Radio Pictures (studio publicity photograph) · Public domain · Source

  • Play Cheek to Cheek from the licensed copy. Count cuts; check feet and hem.
  • Then the Pina trailer in the lesson: where does Wenders' camera stand?

Same dance, different film

  • Count cuts while Cheek to Cheek runs; are feet and hem in frame?
  • What does the close-up sell: the dress or the star?

Master Lecture · Dance, cinema and fashion

11 · The public makes the star

Hollywood used fashion photography to turn stars into fashion references.

it's the public who makes the star

(Sill 2008, 127)

Image: Rogers mid-step in a light gown beside Astaire in tails on a shiny dance floor.

Ginger Rogers and Fred Astaire - Follow the Fleet (1936) · RKO Radio Pictures (studio publicity photograph) · Public domain · Source

  • Sill 2008, 130: the star presented as a fashion reference.
  • Ask: who is credited — dancers, costume designer, photographer?

Master Lecture · Dance, cinema and fashion

12 · Learn from the new media

When film arrived, the stage could compete — or learn. So can you, with a phone and Firefly.

a theatre which, instead of competing against the newer means of communication, tries to apply them and to learn from them

(Benjamin 1998, 99)

Play Chomón's Création de la serpentine (1908)

Image: A Muybridge frame: a woman in a light dress dancing before a gridded wall.

Eadweard Muybridge, Animal Locomotion, Woman Dancing (fancy), 1887, plate 187 · Eadweard Muybridge · Public domain · Source

  • Segundo de Chomón (Teruel 1871 – Paris 1929): the edit, not the dancer, transforms the costume.
  • Bridge to I.8 animation.

Master Lecture · Dance, cinema and fashion

13 · Climb only as high as your evidence

Looks-like is rung 1. A title, a dated record, testimony climb higher.

Image: La Argentina mid-dance in a long ruffled bata de cola, one arm raised.

La Argentina dancing LOC agc.7a09934 · Arnold Genthe · Public domain · Source

  • Forsythe × Miyake: costumes 1991/92 → Pleats Please 1993 (rung 3).
  • Appropriation: who is credited, paid, displaced?

How do we know a movement travelled?

  • Rung 1 needs only eyes; rung 4 needs testimony, dates and works.
  • Appropriation is a question of power, not a rung.

Master Lecture · Dance, cinema and fashion

14 · Madrid → Tokyo

Kazuo Ohno's 1977 solo is titled Admiring La Argentina. When did he see her? 1926, 1927, 1929 — sources disagree.

Watch at source: Numeridanse

Image: Max Slevogt’s painting of La Argentina standing hands on hips, a pale shawl embroidered with large pink and green flowers over a ruffled dress.

Slevogt La Argentina · Max Slevogt · Public domain · Source

  • The title is a quotation you can check (rung 2).
  • What does Ohno quote: a costume, a gesture, a feeling?
  • Slevogt (Berlin) and Ohno (Tokyo) both answer one Spanish dancer: another travel route to map.

Master Lecture · Dance, cinema and fashion

15 · Who performs whose culture?

An American dancer presents herself as a Hindu goddess for Western audiences.

Image: Ruth St. Denis in a jewelled, fringed costume, arms extended, holding small cymbals.

Ruth St. Denis in Radha. (3110871798) · Otto Sarony · Public domain · Source

  • Who is named, paid or displaced when a practice enters a new market?
  • What record separates influence from appropriation?

Master Lecture · Dance, cinema and fashion

16 · Shock on the red carpet

Matières Fécales built a name on disgust — then dressed a Hollywood star for the 2026 Met Gala.

Open the label's Depop shop (new tab)

Critique, or a new kind of luxury? Bring evidence, not adjectives.

Image: Sarah Paulson on mossy museum steps in a voluminous grey tulle gown with a feathered bodice.

Guests at the 2026 Met Gala 354 · SWinxy (photograph); Matières Fécales (gown) · CC BY 4.0 · Source

  • Abjection is a theory of who is pushed out, not a synonym for 'shocking'.
  • Also discuss Delfín and Locking only with evidence: statements, reception, who wore it.

Master Lecture · Dance, cinema and fashion

17 · Butoh has histories, not one look

White paint is the easiest thing to copy and the least informative. A pose cannot say where a movement came from.

Image: Sankai Juku dancers with whitened bodies crouch on a dark stage; three robed figures stand behind.

Sankai Juku · Carlos de las Piedras · CC BY 2.0 · Source

  • Second-generation butoh (Amagatsu, 1975) on a Mexican stage; long reception in Argentina too.
  • Who can name a tradition, who earns from its circulation?

Recall check

Alone, from memory, 3 minutes. Then compare with a partner.

  1. Name the four things a garment can do to movement.
  2. Why are most early 'Fuller' films not evidence of Fuller?
  3. What does a full-figure frame show that a close-up hides?
  4. Which rung is 'it looks like' on the evidence ladder?
  5. Whose name is in the title of Ohno's 1977 solo?

Course geometric background · threshold · #c378606cc29b · Original course SVG

Answers:

  • Drape, extension, tension, reorganisation.
  • The serpentine was copied: Annabelle, unnamed Lumière dancer, Pathé copy.
  • Feet, hem, the whole garment in motion.
  • Rung 1: visual analogy — never enough alone.
  • Antonia Mercé, La Argentina.

Burst → layers → one image of time

  • C2 burst of about 12 frames → keep 6 → Photoshop layers at 25% or Lighten (T1).
